225.title: Pauri 36, meaning: the realm of effort
225.hook: knowledge blazes; then comes the realm of effort, where beauty shapes mind and understanding (Japji 36)
225.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 36 describes Saram Khand, the third of the five realms, which Sikh teachers variously explain as the realm of effort, of humility, or of spiritual joy, where the mind itself is reshaped.

segments.voice: Yesterday, parchandd: in the realm of knowledge, knowledge blazes. Your line was giaan khandd. Today, the next realm, and it's a workshop.

Watch someone learn the violin. The first month is painful for everyone in the house: squeaks, scratches, a bow that won't sit straight. But something is happening that you can't hear yet. The fingertips are hardening. The ear is learning to catch a note that's slightly off. Six months in, the student hears music differently, not just plays it differently. Anyone who has trained for anything, a sport, a language, a craft, knows this. You work on the thing, and the thing works on you. Pauri 36 calls the next realm a workshop where exactly that happens.
screen: `A MONTH OF SQUEAKS.` → `THE EAR IS LEARNING.` → `THE THING WORKS ON YOU.`

segments.voice: After knowledge blazes, the stanza turns: saram khandd kee baanee roop. The language of Saram Khand is beauty, is form. Then: tithai ghaarrat gharreeai bahut anoop. There, shaping is done, beyond compare. Gharreeai is what a potter or a smith does, forming something by hand. And what gets shaped? Tithai gharreeai surat mat man budh. There, awareness, intellect, mind and understanding are shaped. Not clay. You. In the realm of knowledge, you saw how big creation is. Here, the seeing gets worked into who you are. In the middle comes a small, honest admission: taa keeaa galaa katheeaa naa jaahi, je ko kahai pichhai pachhutaae. Its matters can't be told; whoever tries will be sorry afterward. Even Nanak refuses to over-describe it. So what does saram mean? Here, teachers honestly differ. Many translators read it as effort or striving, from an old word for labor; that's today's title. Others hear modesty or humility, the same word you met in Pauri 28, where modesty was the yogi's begging bowl. Some read it as spiritual joy. Sikh teachers often hold these together: the humble, beautiful work of being reshaped. Either way, the picture is a workshop, where patient, humble effort lets knowledge reshape the mind.

segments.voice: Picture one small thing you usually rush, washing a pan, writing a message, tying your shoes, listening to someone, and see yourself doing it slowly and well, the way a craftsperson would. Then give the same care to your breath: in fully, out completely, each breath well made.
Saram Khand. The realm of effort, a workshop where beauty is the language and awareness, mind and understanding are shaped. The third of Japji's five realms.
Your line: effort shapes the mind. In this workshop, the one being shaped is you. That's day two hundred twenty-five.

226.title: Pauri 37, sound: karam khandd
226.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 37 describes the last two of the five realms, and its opening, karam khandd kee baanee jor, echoes the frame of the line before it about Saram Khand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saram Khand, the workshop where effort shapes the mind. Today, the fourth realm, sound first.

Songwriters know a trick. Later in a song, you bring back a line's exact shape with one word changed, and the listener's ear lights up. The same frame, a new filling: you've moved, but you're still in the same song. Yesterday's stanza gave a frame: saram khandd kee baanee roop, the language of the realm of effort is beauty. Pauri 37 opens with that same frame, changes two words, and suddenly you're somewhere new. One of the new words is an old friend, the word that hammered through Pauri 33. Listen for the echo.
screen: `THE SAME FRAME, A NEW WORD.` → `SARAM KHANDD KEE BAANEE ROOP.` → `LISTEN FOR THE ECHO.`

segments.voice: Here is the first line of Pauri 37: karam khandd kee baanee jor. Same frame: saram becomes karam; roop becomes jor. Karam: grace, generosity, kindness freely given. It came into Punjabi through Persian, and it's easy to confuse with karma, which means action and its results. Both appear in the Granth. Here the usual reading is grace, though some commentators read it as deeds. Karam khandd: the realm of grace. Kee baanee: its language, its mark. Jor: power, strength. The language of the realm of grace is power. In Pauri 33, jor hammered through every line with no beside it: no power to speak, no power to be silent, no power of our own. Here jor comes back, and there's no no. The power that wasn't ours is at home in the realm of grace. Then the second line: tithai hor na koee hor. Tithai: there. Hor: other, else. Na koee: not anyone. Hor again. There, no one else, no other at all. Hor bookends the line, the way jor boxed in the lines of Pauri 33. Say the two lines aloud and a strong, even beat comes through. Tomorrow, who lives in this realm, and what lies beyond it.
screen: `SARAM BECOMES KARAM.` · `KARAM — GRACE, NOT KARMA.` · `JOR — POWER, AND NO NO THIS TIME.` · `TITHAI HOR NA KOEE HOR.` · then, large: `KARAM KHANDD.`

segments.voice: Say the two lines aloud three times with a strong, even beat: karam khandd kee baanee jor, tithai hor na koee hor. Then say yesterday's line once, saram khandd kee baanee roop, and today's once more, and hear the echo. Sit in silence after, letting the beat fade with each breath out, resting without trying to earn anything.
Hor, other, else. It opens in the realm of grace: karam khandd kee baanee jor, its language is power, and there is no one else, no other at all.
Your line: karam khandd, the realm of grace. Saram became karam, and jor came home. Day two hundred twenty-six, done.

227.title: Pauri 37, meaning: grace and truth
227.hook: in the realm of grace dwell the mighty in spirit; in the realm of truth dwells the Formless, beholding all (Japji 37)
227.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 37 describes Karam Khand, the realm of grace, and Sach Khand, the realm of truth where the Formless dwells, and ends with Nanak saying that describing it is as hard as steel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hor, other, from the line tithai hor na koee hor: in the realm of grace, karam khandd, there is no one else. Today, that realm opened, and the last realm of all.

Describe your mother's voice, or your grandfather's laugh, to someone who never heard it. A few words come: warm, a bit low, it cracks at the end. Then the words run out, because they're so much smaller than the thing. Knowing and telling are different skills, and some things only allow one of them. Two stanzas ago, Saram Khand warned that its matters can't be told. Pauri 37 climbs to the very top of the Japji's ladder, and there Guru Nanak meets that wall again, harder than before.
screen: `DESCRIBE A VOICE YOU LOVE.` → `THE WORDS ARE TOO SMALL.` → `KNOWING ISN'T TELLING.`

segments.voice: Who lives in the realm of grace? Tithai jodh mahaabal soor: warriors of great strength, heroes, and the Lord, here called Raam, a name the Granth uses for the One who fills everything, is completely present in them. They neither die nor are deceived, the stanza says, those in whose minds the One lives. Devotees of many worlds dwell there, full of joy, the True One in their hearts. That's the fourth realm, Karam Khand. Then the fifth, the top of the ladder: sach khandd vasai nirankaar. In the realm of truth dwells the Formless One. And what does the Formless do there? Kar kar vekhai nadar nihaal: creating, He watches over it all, and blesses with a glance. You heard that watching in Pauris 30 and 31; here it's at home. In Sach Khand there are continents, worlds and universes without end; worlds upon worlds of forms, each moving as the order moves it. He sees, He is delighted, He reflects. And then Nanak stops. Nanak kathnaa karrarraa saar. To describe it is as hard as steel. Saar is steel, iron: you could chew on it forever and not bite through. In Pauri 36 the words fell short; here they meet steel. Some Sikh teachers describe Sach Khand not only as a place after this life but as a state to be touched now, in the heart, when the Formless is near.
screen: `KARAM KHAND — THE MIGHTY IN SPIRIT.` · `SACH KHAND — THE FORMLESS DWELLS.` · `HE WATCHES, BLESSING WITH A GLANCE.` · `KATHNAA KARRARRAA SAAR.` · then, large: `HARD AS STEEL TO TELL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the things you're grateful for, one at a time, without describing them: a face, a meal, a morning, a voice. Let each one arrive, feel the thanks, and let it go; if a word comes, let it pass too. When the list runs out, rest in the thanks itself.
Sach Khand. The realm of truth, where the Formless One dwells, creating and watching with a kindly glance. The fifth realm, the top of the ladder, and too hard to tell.
Your line: hard as steel to tell. Where the words run out, silence is enough. See you tomorrow.

228.title: Pauri 38, sound: jat paahaaraa
228.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 38, the last stanza before the closing salok, uses the tools of a goldsmith's workshop, furnace, anvil and crucible, as a picture of the disciplined life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sach Khand, the realm of truth, hard as steel to tell. Today, the thirty-eighth and last pauri of the Japji.
screen: `SACH KHAND — HARD AS STEEL TO TELL.`

segments.voice: An old Punjabi bazaar, and down one side, a goldsmiths' lane. Tiny shops, open to the street. In each, someone sits cross-legged on the floor beside a small furnace, blowing on the coals through a pipe until they glow orange. A little anvil, a row of hammers, a pair of tongs, and the steady tap, tap, tap of metal being coaxed into shape. The work is slow. Hurry it, and the gold cracks. Guru Nanak's hearers would have known shops like these the way you know a coffee shop. In the last pauri of the Japji, he walks you into one.
screen: `THE GOLDSMITHS' LANE.` → `A SMALL FURNACE, A LITTLE ANVIL.` → `TAP, TAP, TAP.`

segments.voice: Pauri 38 opens: jat paahaaraa dheeraj suniaar. Four words, each a piece of the workshop. Jat: self-restraint, holding yourself in check. Paahaaraa: the smith's furnace, the forge. Let restraint be the furnace. Dheeraj: patience, steadiness; you'll hear it in Punjabi and Hindi today, when someone tells you to keep calm and wait. Suniaar: the goldsmith; in Punjab a jeweler is still called a sunaar. Let patience be the goldsmith. Now the rhythm. Jat, one short hit. Paahaaraa, long and rolling, like breath on the coals. Dheeraj, firm. Suniaar, opening out at the end. A strike, a long breath, a strike, a long breath, like the work itself. Then the next line keeps building the shop: aharan mat, ved hatheeaar. Aharan: the anvil. Mat: understanding, good sense. Ved: here, knowledge. Hatheeaar: tools. Let understanding be the anvil and knowledge the tools. The whole Japji began with Guru Nanak saying that thinking a hundred thousand times won't get you there. Now, at the very end, he gives you a place to work: not a temple of thought but a workshop of patience. Tomorrow, what gets made in it.
screen: `JAT PAAHAARAA — RESTRAINT, THE FURNACE.` · `DHEERAJ SUNIAAR — PATIENCE, THE GOLDSMITH.` · `A STRIKE, A LONG BREATH.` · `AHARAN MAT — UNDERSTANDING, THE ANVIL.` · then, large: `JAT PAAHAARAA.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, slowly, three times: jat paahaaraa dheeraj suniaar, with jat short like a tap on metal and paahaaraa long like a slow breath on coals; then add aharan mat, ved hatheeaar, once. Afterward, breathe like a goldsmith working the fire: a slow, steady breath out, as if gently blowing on coals, and a quiet breath in, no rushing.
Suniaar, the goldsmith. The last pauri of the Japji opens in a goldsmith's shop: restraint is the furnace, patience the goldsmith, understanding the anvil.
Your line: jat paahaaraa, restraint is the furnace. In this shop, patience does the work. Until tomorrow.

229.title: Pauri 38, meaning: the true mint
229.hook: let restraint be the furnace, patience the goldsmith, love the crucible; there the Word is minted (Japji 38)
229.tomorrow: The final salok: air, water, earth
229.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 38 ends with the Word minted in the true mint, and Sikhs honor the shabad as the Guru, present in the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, suniaar, the goldsmith, and your line: jat paahaaraa, restraint is the furnace. Today, what the workshop makes.

Pick up any coin and look closely. There's a stamp on it: a face, a date, a design pressed into the metal with enormous force. That stamp is the whole point. A plain disc is just metal; a struck coin is something people will trust, pass from hand to hand, and spend. Counterfeiters fake the stamp, so people learned to test coins: ringing them on a counter, weighing them, even biting them. A true coin comes from a true mint. The last line of the last pauri says what's being struck.
screen: `A COIN AND ITS STAMP.` → `TESTING FOR FAKES.` → `A TRUE COIN, A TRUE MINT.`

segments.voice: The workshop so far: restraint the furnace, patience the goldsmith, understanding the anvil, knowledge the tools. The stanza keeps going. Bhau khalaa: awe is the bellows, the deep reverence that keeps the fire breathing. Agan tap taau: discipline is the fire's heat. Bhaandaa bhaau: love is the crucible, the vessel that holds the molten metal, and into it amrit, the nectar, is poured. Then the line everything was building toward: gharreeai sabad sachee ttakasaal. In this true mint, the Word is struck. Sabad, sometimes written shabad, is the Word: the Guru's word, the hymns of the Granth, and for Sikhs something more, because the Guru and the shabad are understood as one. That's why Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru. So what does it mean to mint the Word? It isn't only read or sung. It's stamped into a life, by heat and patience and love, until that life is a coin other people can trust. Then the stanza's last lines: jin kau nadar karam tin kaar. This is the work of those on whom the glance of grace falls. Nanak nadaree nadar nihaal: the Gracious One, with a glance, fills them with joy. In the stanza's picture, the tools are there to be used, and the stamp comes by grace.

segments.voice: Picture one moment when you'll need patience: a slow line, a child's question for the fifth time, a coworker who takes forever. See yourself as the goldsmith there, not rushing the metal, keeping the fire steady. Breathe like the bellows, a long breath out and a quiet breath in, and let the patience settle into your hands and jaw.
Sabad. The Word: the Guru's word, and for Sikhs the Guru itself, struck into a life in the true mint of restraint, patience, awe and love.
Your line: the word is minted. A true coin, from a true mint. Day two hundred twenty-nine, done.

230.title: The final salok: air, water, earth
230.hook: pavan guru paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother; day and night the nurses (Japji, salok)
230.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib every morning, ending with this closing salok, and its first line is often quoted by Sikhs speaking about care for the environment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sabad, in the last pauri: the word is minted. Today, the short verse that closes the whole Japji.

The first few minutes of your life. Before you had a name, before you knew anyone's face, three things met you. Air rushed into your lungs, and you cried. Water: you'd floated in it for months, and someone washed you in it. Then you were laid down, held, on something solid. Air, water, ground: there before any teacher, any parent's voice, any word, and there again every morning since, without being asked. After thirty-eight stanzas of climbing, the Japji doesn't end at the top of the ladder. It ends with one short verse that comes all the way back down to these three.
screen: `YOUR FIRST MINUTES.` → `AIR, WATER, GROUND.` → `THE JAPJI COMES BACK DOWN.`

segments.voice: The Japji opened with a salok, a short verse, before the first pauri: aad sach, true in the beginning. It closes with one more: pavan guroo paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat. Air is the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother. Air as Guru is worth a moment. The breath carries every word, every hymn, every sound of the Name; without air, no teaching reaches anyone. Then: divas raat due daaee daaiaa, khelai sagal jagat. Day and night are the two nurses, a woman and a man who care for a child, and in their lap the whole world plays. A family picture of creation: parents, nurses, and all of us, children, playing. Then the tone turns serious. Good and bad deeds are read out in the presence of Dharam, the righteous judge. By their own actions, some come near, some stay far. And the last lines: those who remembered the Name have finished their hard work and gone. Nanak says, their faces shine, and many others are set free along with them. Many Sikhs today quote pavan guroo paanee pitaa when they speak about caring for the earth: if the air is your teacher and the earth your mother, you don't treat them like trash. And notice where the Japji leaves you. Not in a far realm, but right here, breathing, drinking, standing on the ground.
screen: `PAVAN GUROO — AIR IS THE GURU.` · `WATER THE FATHER, EARTH THE MOTHER.` · `DAY AND NIGHT, THE TWO NURSES.` · `FACES SHINE, AND OTHERS GO FREE.` · then, large: `AIR, WATER, EARTH.`

segments.voice: If you can, open a window or step outside; if not, stay where you are, and breathe in slowly, feeling the air come in, the Guru in the salok's picture. Take a sip of water if you have some, then press your feet into the floor, into the earth beneath the building. Stay with the breath, letting air, water and earth hold you, the way they did in your first minutes.
Pavan, air, the breath that carries every word. The short verse that closes the Japji: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother, day and night the nurses, and faces that shine.
Your line: air, water, earth. Teacher, father and mother, all around you. That's day two hundred thirty.

231.title: Camp 4 close: the whole Japji
231.hook: thirty-eight pauris and two saloks, from sochai soch to the faces that shine
231.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the whole Japji Sahib every morning as the first bani of Nitnem, often from memory; it stands at the very start of the Guru Granth Sahib, on its first pages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pavan, in the final salok: air, water, earth. Today, the last day of this camp, and a look back at the whole Japji.

Seventy-four days ago, this camp began with an alphabet. Thirty-five letters, the Guru's alphabet, and a promise: you'd hear each stanza before trying to understand it. Then the Mool Mantar, sounded out. Then one word, jap, recite, remember. Then, one pauri at a time, the whole thing. Some people have recited the Japji every morning since childhood; some have never heard a line of it. This path has put you somewhere in between: you've walked it, stanza by stanza, from the first line to the last. That's worth stopping for.
screen: `SEVENTY-FOUR DAYS AGO: AN ALPHABET.` → `ONE PAURI AT A TIME.` → `THE WHOLE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here is the Japji, all of it, in one breath. The Mool Mantar, Ik Onkar, one Creator, and a salok: aad sach, true in the beginning, true now. Pauri 1: sochai soch, thinking a hundred thousand times won't get you there; walk in the hukam, the order. The order holding everything, and haumai, the I, I, that forgets it. The Giver who never tires. The early hours and nadar, the kindly glance. Four stanzas of suniai, listening, and four of mannai, trusting. Asankh, the countless: devotions, fools, names. The ant who remembers. Even hunger counted as a gift. Four stanzas for the yogis: contentment for earrings, wisdom for food, the One who sees though unseen, storehouses filled once, for all. Then the ladder: one tongue becoming millions, the steps to the Beloved, no power of our own. The five realms: Dharam Khand, this earth, a house for right action. Gian Khand, so many worlds. Saram Khand, the workshop where effort shapes the mind. Karam Khand, grace. Sach Khand, where the Formless dwells, hard as steel to tell. The goldsmith's shop where the Word is minted. And the closing salok: air the Guru, water the father, earth the mother, and faces that shine. Thirty-eight pauris and two saloks. Next, a new camp: the depths, stepping back from the Japji to see the whole Guru Granth Sahib: how it's built, whose voices are in it, and its great themes.
screen: `MOOL MANTAR AND AAD SACH.` · `LISTENING, TRUSTING, THE COUNTLESS.` · `THE YOGIS, THE LADDER.` · `FIVE REALMS, AND THE TRUE MINT.` · then, large: `I ACTUALLY READ IT.`

segments.voice: Let the stanzas come back on their own, in any order: the ant, the storehouses, the goldsmith's furnace, suniai, by listening. Whatever line surfaces, let it sit with you, say it quietly if you remember it, then let another come. If none comes, simply rest, breathing, in the quiet the Japji leaves behind.
Jap, recite, remember, the Japji's own title. The whole thing, thirty-eight pauris and two saloks, walked one stanza at a time, from sochai soch to the faces that shine.
Your line: I actually read it. From sochai soch to the faces that shine. Camp four, complete.
